review.headline: Your design copes on a normal day but collapses at peak because every check hits the database.

items.text: Every check goes straight to the database, so at peak you ask for 10,050 calls a second from a store that can serve at most 2,509 calls a second. The database runs at 401 % of capacity and tail latency breaks the promise.
items.ask: What store would let a check write stay fast when peak load lands on it?

items.text: The database is also a single point of failure. With no spare, losing it stops both checks and usage reads, so one failure takes the whole limiter down.
items.ask: How would you keep checks answering if the database went away?

items.text: On a normal afternoon the design passes with 11 % to spare on its tightest promise. The basic shape works when load stays low.

next.text: Take checks off the database and put the counter in a store suited to fast writes under peak load, then rerun the evening peak test.

The db receives {{finding:overloaded:GET_FEED:db.actual}} against a limit of {{finding:overloaded:GET_FEED:db.expected}}, so it runs at {{finding:overloaded:GET_FEED:db.rho}}. That overload pushes your feed reads over the latency promise. The cache in the path is not protecting the db enough at peak.

In the morning test you pass with {{test:t01-morning.spare}} to spare on your tightest promise. That shows the basic path can work when load is lower. The issue is not the shape at low load. It is headroom when many opens arrive together.

items.ask: How could the cache serve more of those opens before they reach the db?
items.text: The cache stays almost idle while the db saturates. At peak the cache is at {{load:cache.peak}} and the api layer is at {{load:api.peak}}, while the db is at {{load:db.peak}}. You have headroom in the wrong places. Moving work away from the db is the direction to explore.

items.text: Reads also fail in that same event, so a single storage loss hurts both writing and opening the feed. Your app servers survive on their own, but the feed depends on the store that has gone.

items.text: Your read path is comfortably fast in both passing load tests, with median {{path:GET_FEED.p50}} and tail latency {{path:GET_FEED.p99}}. That gives you headroom for the extra work a safer write path may add.

review.headline: Your design is invalid because neither the feed read nor the post write reaches a store that holds data.

items.text: Your feed read cannot work as drawn. The judge found GET_FEED never reaches a place where the data lives at 5. You need to route that request through your app layer to a store that holds the feed, or the open returns nothing.
items.ask: Where should GET_FEED end, and which store holds each feed?

items.text: Your write path also cannot work. POST is never saved because its route does not reach a store at 6. Until a post is durably stored, no feed rebuild can happen and the accepted post can be lost.
items.ask: Where should POST be written first, and how do feeds learn about it?

items.text: Because both paths are disconnected, the judge marked the whole design invalid with 2 errors. Fix the wiring first before you tune caching or latency, as no performance claim can be judged on a design that does not connect.

next.text: Reconnect both paths to a store first. Make POST save durably, then make GET_FEED read the stored feed, and resubmit before you consider freshness or speed.

review.headline: Your design is sound in steady load but fails the spike because the database is on the direct write path.

items.text: Your design fails the spike because SEND hits the database directly. The database got 5,000 calls a second but can serve at most 2,500 calls a second, so requests queue instead of being accepted at once. You need to decouple acceptance from the database write.
items.ask: How would you accept writes during a spike without writing to the database straight away?

items.text: The database is also the wrong place to absorb bursts. It runs at 20 % in steady load but peaks at 200 % in The match starts, so any spike will saturate it first.
items.ask: What would you put between accepting a send and recording it in the database?

items.text: In steady load you pass, with 20 % to spare on your tightest promise. Latency on SEND is fine at {{path:SEND.p99}} at the tail, so the basic path is sound.

next.text: Next, move the database off the immediate SEND path so a spike can be accepted and drained in the background within the delivery window.

items.text: Your promise was never repeating names, yet the judge expects {{finding:collision:UPLOAD_IMAGE:ids.actual}} repeats from short random ids. At this scale collisions become likely, so different photos can overwrite or confuse each other.
The judge recorded total failure in the afternoon test, so nothing in this design can be called proven yet. The name collision alone explains that failure and blocks further scaling work.

next.text: Start with the ids part and widen its names so repeats cannot occur, then rerun the same afternoon test to check the fix.

review.headline: You meet view latency but cost is far over budget because the app tier carries every read.

items.text: Your design costs ₹2,47,000 a month against a budget of ₹60,000, so it fails on cost alone. The app tier is 97 % of the total at ₹2,40,000. That tier is where your money is going, so it is the first place to cut.
items.ask: How would you serve most views without paying for the app tier each time?

items.text: Your read path goes through the app tier and file store for every view, as shown by cdn 15.0 ms → lb 2.0 ms → api 20.1 ms → files 40.0 ms. The CDN carries little traffic at 0 % and costs ₹3,000. Serving repeat views from the edge would shift load away from the costly tier while keeping latency healthy at {{path:GET_IMAGE.p99}}.

review.headline: Accepted design with strong resilience and cost as the tightest margin.

items.text: You passed every test, and the budget is your tightest promise with 12 % to spare at ₹1,67,000 against a budget of ₹1,90,000. That margin leaves little room for growth, so treat cost as your main constraint.

items.text: You kept working when a server died, when the database primary failed, and when the cache restarted. That shows your stateless tier and your recovery path are sound under pressure.

items.text: During the match your api reached 60 % and your db reached 48 % of what they can take. That still leaves headroom for peaks, though api is the tier to watch first.

items.text: Your top list read stays fast with a latency of {{path:GET_TOP.p99}} and your cache is lightly loaded at 6 % at peak. Caching the small set of live games is doing the heavy lifting for reads.

review.headline: Your database is overloaded during the match because top reads reach it too often.

items.text: During the match the database receives 1,260 calls a second but it can serve at most 1,050 calls a second. That overload makes the verdict fail and it is caused by GET_TOP reads.
